newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria seeks help from Russians on hidden arms.
newsitem.headline: Austria seeks help from Russians on hidden arms.

text.p: Austria said on Wednesday it would seek Russian help in locating Cold War arms depots that may be peppered across the Alpine countryside.
Interior Minister Karl Schloegl said he would follow "diplomatic channels" in his efforts to trace the stashes of guns and explosives, thought to have been concealed by a foreign power.

The authorities knew of one explosives dump outside Salzburg in western Austria and several smaller stashes, containing one or two handguns, in the east of the country, Schloegl told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
"We will try to get further information from the Russians on whether there are any more depots," he said.
"We believe the stashes contain mines and fuses intended for use by foreign agents. We cannot prove which secret service was responsible but we have our suspicions."
News of the concealed weapons surfaced at the weekend when current affairs magazine Profil reported that Soviet KGB agents had buried explosives for use in sabotage attacks.
The revelation came one year after the United States admitted it had stockpiled arms in 79 arsenals across Austria in the early 1950s, as part of a defence strategy in case of a Soviet invasion.
Most of the U.S. depots, containing thousands of tonnes of explosives and hundreds of pieces of artillery, have since been found and made safe.

Austria was split into four Allied occupation zones at the end of World War Two. Straddling east and western Europe, it was the ideal location for Soviet and U.S. agents to enact their Cold War drama.
Allied troops withdrew in 1955 when Austria enshrined neutrality in its post war constitution and Moscow was satisfied it posed no threat to neighbouring Soviet Bloc states.
Schloegl, a Social Democrat, conceded there had been a breakdown of communication between the police and government ministers over the latest weapons dumps.
Austrian state police learned of the arsenals' existence last year but did not pass on the information.
"I have taken steps to ensure that I am thoroughly informed of such important matters in the future," Schloegl said.
Conservative politicians have attacked the authorities' handling of the matter and accused the police of by-passing democratic procedures.
"The state police must not be a state within a state," said Andreas Khol, conservative whip of junior coalition partner the People's Party.
